rubric.minimum_fix: Four evidence: (1) size/shape similar to bacteria; (2) double membrane (inner = bacterial membrane with cardiolipin); (3) circular naked mitochondrial DNA; (4) 70S ribosomes (sensitive to bacterial antibiotics). Gene transfer: most mitochondrial genes transferred to nucleus over evolution (endosymbiotic gene transfer) for better regulation, protection, and coordination.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe two or three lines of evidence for endosymbiosis (double membrane, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission).
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Four lines of evidence: (1) Size and shape: mitochondria are similar in size (~1-2 μm) and shape to alpha-proteobacteria; (2) Double membrane: mitochondria have two membranes — the outer membrane likely derived from the phagocytic vacuole; the inner membrane is the original bacterial plasma membrane with bacterial-type lipid composition (cardiolipin); (3) Mitochondrial DNA: circular, naked DNA (like bacterial chromosomes) located in the matrix; not associated with histones; encodes rRNA, tRNA, and some proteins; (4) Mitochondrial ribosomes: 70S ribosomes (bacterial type) sensitive to antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes (chloramphenicol, erythromycin) but not 80S eukaryotic ribosomes; (5) Binary fission: mitochondria divide by binary fission, not mitosis; (6) Phylogenetic similarity: mitochondrial rRNA sequences are closely related to alpha-proteobacteria (specifically Rickettsia-like organisms). Any four with correct explanation. (ii) Gene transfer to nucleus: over evolutionary time, most ancestral bacterial genes were transferred to the host cell nucleus (endosymbiotic gene transfer). This is adaptive because: nuclear genes can be regulated by eukaryotic gene expression machinery; nuclear DNA is protected by repair mechanisms; reduced mtDNA reduces the risk of harmful mutations in the energy-producing organelle; nuclear-encoded proteins are imported post-translationally into mitochondria via TOM/TIM complexes.

rubric.minimum_fix: H⁺ pumped from matrix to intermembrane space by Complexes I (4H⁺), III (4H⁺), IV (2H⁺) as electrons flow. Proton gradient (proton-motive force) drives H⁺ back through ATP synthase F₀ channel → F₁ rotation → ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi. Complex IV reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain (i) proton gradient source, (ii) how it drives ATP synthase, (iii) the general role of ETC complexes in building the gradient -- score (i)/(ii)/(iii) separately.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Source of proton gradient: NADH and FADH₂ (from glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle) donate electrons to the ETC. As electrons pass through the complexes, the energy released is used to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space: Complex I pumps 4H⁺, Complex III pumps 4H⁺, Complex IV pumps 2H⁺. This creates an electrochemical proton gradient (high H⁺/low pH in intermembrane space vs. matrix) = proton-motive force. ATP synthesis: H⁺ cannot freely cross the inner membrane (impermeable). H⁺ flows back down its electrochemical gradient through the F₀ channel of ATP synthase (the only route). H⁺ flow drives rotation of the F₀ rotor → mechanical rotation transmitted to F₁ catalytic subunits → conformational changes in F₁ catalyze ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi (rotary catalysis). Specific roles: Complex I — accepts electrons from NADH → passes to ubiquinone, pumps 4H⁺; Complex III — accepts electrons from reduced ubiquinone (QH₂) via Q-cycle → passes to cytochrome c, pumps 4H⁺; Complex IV — accepts electrons from cytochrome c → reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor), pumps 2H⁺; ATP synthase — H⁺ gradient drives F₀ rotation → F₁ synthesizes ATP (chemiosmosis).

rubric.minimum_fix: Rotenone: O₂ decreases (ETC blocked at Complex I), ATP decreases. Oligomycin: O₂ decreases (back-pressure stops ETC), ATP decreases. DNP: O₂ increases (no back-pressure, ETC runs faster), ATP decreases (gradient dissipated as heat).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict rotenone (decreases both), oligomycin (ATP synthesis decreases; O2 consumption also decreases per the stimulus note on coupled electron flow, or unaffected with sound reasoning accepted), and DNP (O2 consumption increases, ATP synthesis decreases) with reasoning for each.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Rotenone (blocks Complex I): electron flow from NADH through Complex I is blocked → electrons cannot enter the ETC from NADH → H⁺ pumping by Complexes I, III, IV stops → proton gradient collapses → ATP synthesis stops. O₂ consumption DECREASES (Complex IV cannot receive electrons; O₂ is not reduced). ATP synthesis DECREASES (no gradient). (ii) Oligomycin (blocks F₀ of ATP synthase): H⁺ cannot flow through ATP synthase → H⁺ accumulates in intermembrane space → proton gradient INCREASES (back-pressure) → this back-pressure slows H⁺ pumping by Complexes → electron flow through ETC slows → O₂ consumption DECREASES. ATP synthesis DECREASES (synthase blocked). Classic observation: oligomycin paradoxically reduces O₂ consumption by back-pressure on the ETC. (iii) DNP (uncoupler): makes inner membrane permeable to H⁺ → H⁺ flows back into matrix bypassing ATP synthase → proton gradient dissipated as heat → no ATP synthesized. But now there is no back-pressure on the ETC → ETC pumps H⁺ as fast as possible to try to maintain gradient → O₂ consumption INCREASES dramatically. ATP synthesis DECREASES (to zero — all gradient dissipated as heat). DNP causes hyperthermia (was used as a diet drug — dangerously). 1 pt per any two correctly predicted and explained.

rubric.minimum_fix: Heart/neurons have high continuous ATP demand → many mitochondria; cristae (inner membrane folds) increase surface area for ETC/ATP synthase. Fission inhibition: neurons need small mitochondria transported to distant synapses via microtubules; without fission, elongated mitochondria cannot enter axons/dendrites → synapses lack ATP → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and divide frequently — less dependent on mitochondrial transport.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why heart cells need many mitochondria and describe cristae as the structural feature that maximizes ATP output.
rubric.evidence_requirements: High energy demand cells: heart muscle and neurons are continuously active and cannot undergo anaerobic metabolism for sustained periods. They require constant high-rate ATP production (heart: ~30 kg ATP/day; neurons: cannot tolerate even brief energy deficits). More mitochondria = more ETC surface area = more ATP. Structural feature: cristae (inner membrane folds) dramatically increase the surface area of the inner membrane → more ETC complexes and ATP synthases per mitochondrion → greater ATP output per organelle. Fission inhibition in neurons vs. fibroblasts: mitochondria must be distributed throughout the cell to local sites of energy demand — in neurons, this means delivering mitochondria to synapses (far from the cell body, up to 1 meter in motor neurons). Mitochondrial fission allows small mitochondria to be transported along microtubules to distant synaptic sites. Without fission: mitochondria become elongated and cannot be transported into dendrites and axons → synapses lack local energy supply → synaptic transmission fails → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and rapidly dividing; mitochondria can be inherited by daughter cells even without efficient transport; fibroblasts are less dependent on precise organelle localization. 1 pt for heart/neurons high demand + cristae explanation; 1 pt for fission/transport mechanism in neurons.

question.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria evolved from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
Describe TWO OR THREE specific lines of evidence that support the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.

Part B: Describe the role of the inner mitochondrial membrane in ATP synthesis. In your answer, explain: (i) the source of the proton gradient; (ii) how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase; and (iii) the general role of the electron transport chain complexes (supplied in the stimulus) in building that gradient.

Part C: A researcher adds the following compounds to isolated mitochondria respiring aerobically. For each compound, predict whether O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis will increase, decrease, or be unaffected, and explain your reasoning:
Rotenone (inhibits Complex I electron transfer)
Oligomycin (blocks the F₀ channel of ATP synthase)
Dinitrophenol / DNP (uncoupler — makes the inner membrane permeable to H⁺)

Part D: Heart muscle cells have unusually high numbers of mitochondria. Explain the functional reason for this, and describe the specific structural feature of mitochondria that maximizes ATP output.
question.stimulus:
Mitochondrial structure:
• Outer membrane: permeable to small molecules (porins)
• Intermembrane space: H⁺ accumulates here during electron transport
• Inner membrane: highly folded into cristae; contains electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase; impermeable to ions
• Matrix: contains Krebs cycle enzymes, mtDNA, mitochondrial ribosomes

The electron transport chain complexes in the inner membrane pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space as electrons pass through them; ATP synthase uses the resulting H⁺ gradient to synthesize ATP. Note: when the H⁺ gradient cannot be relieved by ATP synthase (e.g. if ATP synthase is blocked), electron flow through the chain and O₂ consumption also slow, because the chain works against the built-up gradient.

existing_canonical_answer.canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Four lines of evidence for the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria: (1) Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA genome (mtDNA), structurally similar to bacterial chromosomes (circular, not complexed with histones), distinct from the linear, histone-associated nuclear DNA of the eukaryotic host. (2) Mitochondria contain their own ribosomes, which resemble bacterial (70S-type) ribosomes in size and antibiotic sensitivity, rather than the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic host cell. (3) Mitochondria are bounded by a double membrane: the inner membrane is thought to derive from the original engulfed bacterium's own plasma membrane, while the outer membrane is thought to derive from the host cell's plasma membrane/engulfing vesicle formed during the initial phagocytic/endocytic event. (4) Mitochondria reproduce independently of the host cell cycle via binary fission, similar to how free-living bacteria divide, rather than being newly assembled by the cell each time. (Additional supporting evidence: phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial rRNA/protein sequences shows mitochondria are most closely related to a specific group of alpha-proteobacteria.)

(a)(ii) Over evolutionary time, most genes originally present in the free-living bacterial ancestor's genome were transferred from the mitochondrial genome to the host cell's nuclear genome (endosymbiotic/organellar gene transfer); the corresponding proteins are now synthesized in the cytosol by cytoplasmic ribosomes and imported back into the mitochondrion via specific protein-targeting signal sequences. Retaining most genes in the nucleus is advantageous because it allows the cell to centrally coordinate/regulate mitochondrial protein production together with the rest of the cell's needs, benefits from the nucleus's more robust and accurate DNA repair/recombination machinery (mitochondrial DNA has a higher mutation rate and less effective repair), and reduces genomic redundancy — the mitochondrial genome now retains only a small number of genes, typically those encoding highly hydrophobic membrane proteins (e.g., core electron transport chain subunits) that are difficult to import from the cytosol after synthesis.

(b) The source of the proton gradient is the electron transport chain: as electrons from NADH (and FADH2) are passed sequentially through Complexes I, III, and IV, the energy released by these electron transfers is used by each complex to actively pump H+ ions from the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, creating a higher H+ concentration (and more positive charge/lower pH) in the intermembrane space than in the matrix — an electrochemical proton gradient (proton-motive force). This gradient drives ATP synthesis via chemiosmosis: because the inner membrane is impermeable to ions except through specific channels, H+ can flow back down its concentration gradient (from intermembrane space into the matrix) only through the F0 channel of ATP synthase; this proton flow spins the F0 rotor, driving conformational changes in the F1 head that catalyze phosphorylation of ADP + Pi to form ATP.
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): oxidizes NADH back to NAD+, passing the released electrons into the electron transport chain, and pumps 4 H+ into the intermembrane space.
Complex III (cytochrome bc1): continues passing electrons along the chain and pumps 4 H+ into the intermembrane space.
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): accepts electrons from cytochrome c and transfers them to the final electron acceptor, O2, reducing it (with H+ from the matrix) to H2O, and pumps 2 additional H+ into the intermembrane space.
ATP synthase (Complex V): uses the energy of protons flowing back through its F0 channel down the electrochemical gradient to drive the rotary catalytic mechanism of its F1 head, synthesizing ATP from ADP and Pi.

(c)(i) Rotenone (inhibits Complex I): electrons from NADH can no longer enter the electron transport chain at Complex I, blocking electron flow through the chain from that entry point. O2 consumption DECREASES (electrons can no longer reach Complex IV via this pathway at the normal rate), and ATP synthesis DECREASES correspondingly (the proton gradient can no longer be adequately maintained, reducing ATP synthase activity).

(c)(ii) Oligomycin (blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase): protons can no longer flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, so ATP synthesis DECREASES/stops directly. Because the proton gradient can no longer be dissipated through ATP synthase, H+ accumulates in the intermembrane space, increasing the gradient's magnitude/"back pressure" against further proton pumping; this makes continued pumping by the ETC complexes energetically less favorable, so electron transport (and thus O2 consumption) also DECREASES — both O2 consumption and ATP synthesis decrease.

(c)(iii) DNP (uncoupler; makes the inner membrane permeable to H+): protons leak directly back into the matrix across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase entirely, so the proton gradient cannot build up (it is continuously dissipated as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP) — ATP synthesis DECREASES, since protons no longer need to flow through ATP synthase to return to the matrix. However, because the gradient never builds up significant "back pressure," the ETC complexes can pump protons essentially unimpeded, and the cell/mitochondrion compensates for the lost ATP output by increasing the rate of electron transport — so O2 consumption INCREASES, even though little of that respiratory energy is captured as ATP (most is released as heat).

(d) Heart muscle cells and neurons both have unusually high ATP demands: cardiac muscle cells must contract continuously throughout life to pump blood, requiring constant ATP for the actin–myosin contractile machinery, and neurons require large amounts of ATP to maintain ion gradients (via the Na+/K+ ATPase) for generating and propagating action potentials and for synaptic transmission (neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicle trafficking/recycling) — both cell types are highly metabolically active and depend heavily on the efficient, high-ATP-yield process of oxidative phosphorylation. The specific structural feature that maximizes ATP output is the highly folded inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae): these folds greatly increase the surface area of inner membrane available to house electron transport chain complexes and ATP synthase molecules, allowing many more of these proteins to be packed into a given mitochondrial volume, maximizing the rate of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production per mitochondrion.
A drug inhibiting mitochondrial fission would be especially harmful to neurons compared to rapidly dividing cells like skin fibroblasts because neurons are post-mitotic (non-dividing, terminally differentiated) cells with very long axonal and dendritic processes (sometimes over a meter long) that depend on mitochondrial fission (together with fusion) to distribute healthy mitochondria along their length to distant synaptic terminals, where local ATP supply is essential for synaptic function, and fission is also required for mitochondrial quality control (isolating damaged mitochondrial segments for removal via mitophagy). Because neurons cannot dilute or replace damaged/undistributed mitochondria through cell division (unlike rapidly dividing fibroblasts, which continually produce new daughter cells that each receive a fresh partitioned complement of mitochondria during division), blocking fission would cause neurons to progressively accumulate large, dysfunctional, poorly distributed mitochondria that cannot reach distant synapses or be properly quality-controlled, severely impairing neuronal ATP supply and function over time — a problem that dividing fibroblasts are comparatively protected from due to their shorter, simpler geometry and ongoing mitochondrial redistribution through cell division.

Because the proton gradient can no longer be dissipated through ATP synthase, H+ accumulates in the intermembrane space, increasing the gradient's magnitude/"back pressure" against further proton pumping; this makes continued pumping by the ETC complexes energetically less favorable, so electron transport (and thus O2 consumption) also DECREASES — both O2 consumption and ATP synthesis decrease.

(c)(iii) DNP (uncoupler; makes the inner membrane permeable to H+): protons leak directly back into the matrix across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase entirely, so the proton gradient cannot build up (it is continuously dissipated as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP) — ATP synthesis DECREASES, since protons no longer need to flow through ATP synthase to return to the matrix. However, because the gradient never builds up significant "back pressure," the ETC complexes can pump protons essentially unimpeded, and the cell/mitochondrion compensates for the lost ATP output by increasing the rate of electron transport — so O2 consumption INCREASES, even though little of that respiratory energy is captured as ATP (most is released as heat).

(d) Heart muscle cells and neurons both have unusually high ATP demands: cardiac muscle cells must contract continuously throughout life to pump blood, requiring constant ATP for the actin–myosin contractile machinery, and neurons require large amounts of ATP to maintain ion gradients (via the Na+/K+ ATPase) for generating and propagating action potentials and for synaptic transmission (neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicle trafficking/recycling) — both cell types are highly metabolically active and depend heavily on the efficient, high-ATP-yield process of oxidative phosphorylation. The specific structural feature that maximizes ATP output is the highly folded inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae): these folds greatly increase the surface area of inner membrane available to house electron transport chain complexes and ATP synthase molecules, allowing many more of these proteins to be packed into a given mitochondrial volume, maximizing the rate of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production per mitochondrion.
A drug inhibiting mitochondrial fission would be especially harmful to neurons compared to rapidly dividing cells like skin fibroblasts because neurons are post-mitotic (non-dividing, terminally differentiated) cells with very long axonal and dendritic processes (sometimes over a meter long) that depend on mitochondrial fission (together with fusion) to distribute healthy mitochondria along their length to distant synaptic terminals, where local ATP supply is essential for synaptic function, and fission is also required for mitochondrial quality control (isolating damaged mitochondrial segments for removal via mitophagy). Because neurons cannot dilute or replace damaged/undistributed mitochondria through cell division (unlike rapidly dividing fibroblasts, which continually produce new daughter cells that each receive a fresh partitioned complement of mitochondria during division), blocking fission would cause neurons to progressively accumulate large, dysfunctional, poorly distributed mitochondria that cannot reach distant synapses or be properly quality-controlled, severely impairing neuronal ATP supply and function over time — a problem that dividing fibroblasts are comparatively protected from due to their shorter, simpler geometry and ongoing mitochondrial redistribution through cell division.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain at least two general reasons actual ATP yield is lower than theoretical maximum.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Three reasons actual < theoretical: (1) Proton leak: the inner mitochondrial membrane is not perfectly impermeable; some H⁺ leaks back across without passing through ATP synthase → energy dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP → fewer ATP per NADH/FADH₂. (2) ATP transport cost: ATP synthesized in the mitochondrial matrix must be exported by the ATP-ADP translocase (adenine nucleotide translocator, ANT) using a H⁺ cotransport mechanism → importing ADP and exporting ATP consumes some of the proton-motive force that could otherwise drive ATP synthesis. rubric.minimum_fix: Pasteur effect: anaerobic = 8× more glucose consumed. Aerobic: ETC produces ~30 ATP/glucose; high ATP inhibits PFK-1 → glycolysis slows. Anaerobic: no ETC → only 2 ATP/glucose; low ATP → PFK-1 uninhibited → glycolysis runs fast; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ to keep glycolysis going. Net: must consume much more glucose to maintain ATP.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain increased anaerobic glucose consumption via ATP needs, fermentation's lower yield, and NAD+ regeneration.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Pasteur effect: aerobic conditions → low glucose consumption; anaerobic → 8× higher glucose consumption to maintain same ATP production rate. Mechanism: Under aerobic conditions: pyruvate enters Krebs/ETC → ~30-32 ATP per glucose; glycolysis is regulated at phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) — allosterically inhibited by high ATP/citrate levels → glycolysis slows when ATP is plentiful → low glucose consumption. Under anaerobic conditions: ETC cannot function (no O₂ as terminal electron acceptor) → no oxidative phosphorylation → only 2 ATP per glucose from glycolysis. To compensate: cell must consume 15-16× more glucose to generate the same ATP. But also: without ETC, NADH (from glycolysis) cannot be oxidized → NAD⁺ becomes depleted → glycolysis would halt at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step (requires NAD⁺). Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ (by reducing pyruvate using NADH) → allows glycolysis to continue rapidly. PFK-1 is no longer inhibited (low ATP → low inhibition) → glycolysis runs at maximum rate. Net: high glucose consumption rate required to generate sufficient ATP from inefficient glycolysis alone.

question.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Describe, in general terms, how a glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) is broken down through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle, and identify at which of these stages CO₂ is released.

Part B: For one molecule of glucose completely oxidized through aerobic respiration, explain which stages produce NADH and FADH₂, and explain how these electron carriers are used in the electron transport chain to ultimately produce ATP.

Part C: The actual ATP yield from one glucose molecule is lower than the theoretical maximum. Explain why, describing at least TWO general reasons the process is not perfectly efficient.

Part D: A cell is shifted from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Using the data in Table 1, which shows glucose consumption rates, explain why glucose consumption increases dramatically under anaerobic conditions. Your answer should connect the cell's ATP needs, the lower ATP yield of fermentation compared to aerobic respiration, and the need to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue.
question.stimulus:
Table 1: Glucose consumption in yeast cells
Condition     | Glucose consumed (mmol/hr/g cells)
Aerobic       |        0.5
Anaerobic     |        4.2

General ATP yield summary:
Glycolysis: net 2 ATP (substrate-level), 2 NADH
Pyruvate oxidation: 0 ATP, 2 NADH
Krebs cycle (×2 turns): 2 ATP (GTP), 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂
Each NADH and FADH₂ used in the electron transport chain contributes to ATP production, but not with perfect efficiency.

existing_canonical_answer.canonical_answer_1:
(a) Carbon trace: Glycolysis splits glucose (6C) into 2 pyruvate (3C each); no carbon is lost as CO2 in glycolysis, so all 6 carbons remain in the 2 pyruvate molecules. In pyruvate oxidation, each pyruvate (3C) is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA (2C) plus 1 CO2, releasing 2 CO2 total (one per pyruvate) and leaving 4 carbons in the two acetyl groups. In the Krebs cycle, each acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate; over one turn, 2 CO2 are released via two decarboxylation steps (isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase). Since the cycle turns twice (once per acetyl-CoA), 4 CO2 are released total. Overall CO2 accounting: 2 CO2 (pyruvate oxidation) + 4 CO2 (Krebs, 2 turns) = 6 CO2, accounting for all 6 original glucose carbons.

(b) Electron carriers produced per glucose: Glycolysis produces 2 NADH (cytoplasmic). Pyruvate oxidation produces 2 NADH (mitochondrial matrix, one per pyruvate). The Krebs cycle (2 turns) produces 6 NADH and 2 FADH2. Total = 10 NADH (2 cytoplasmic + 8 mitochondrial) and 2 FADH2. Mitochondrial NADH donates its electrons to Complex I of the electron transport chain, pumping protons at Complexes I, III, and IV (~2.5 ATP equivalent each). FADH2 donates electrons to Complex II, bypassing Complex I, so it only drives proton pumping at Complexes III and IV (~1.5 ATP equivalent each). The 2 cytoplasmic NADH from glycolysis cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly and must be shuttled in via the malate-aspartate shuttle (delivers electrons to mitochondrial NAD+, yielding the full ~2.5 ATP equivalent) or the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (delivers electrons to FAD, yielding only ~1.5 ATP equivalent).

(c) Three reasons actual ATP yield is lower than the theoretical ~30-32 ATP: (1) Proton leak — some protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane through channels other than ATP synthase, dissipating part of the proton-motive force as heat rather than using it to synthesize ATP. (2) Shuttle costs — cytoplasmic NADH shuttled via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers electrons to FAD instead of NAD+, losing about 1 ATP equivalent per cytoplasmic NADH compared to the theoretical maximum that assumes full NADH-level input. (3) The proton gradient is used for purposes other than ATP synthesis, such as powering the transport of ADP into and ATP out of the mitochondrial matrix (via the adenine nucleotide translocase) and importing inorganic phosphate and pyruvate, which consumes some of the gradient's energy without directly producing ATP.

(d) The Pasteur effect: without O2, there is no terminal electron acceptor for the electron transport chain, so oxidative phosphorylation stops and NADH cannot be reoxidized to NAD+ via the ETC. Glycolysis absolutely requires a continuous supply of NAD+ (used by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase); under anaerobic conditions this NAD+ is regenerated instead by fermentation (reducing pyruvate to lactate or acetaldehyde to ethanol), which allows glycolysis to keep running. However, anaerobic glycolysis alone nets only 2 ATP per glucose via substrate-level phosphorylation, versus ~30 ATP aerobically — roughly a 15-fold drop in efficiency. To meet the same cellular energy demand, the cell must dramatically increase glycolytic flux, consistent with Table 1 showing glucose consumption jumping from 0.5 to 4.2 mmol/hr/g (about 8x) under anaerobic conditions. This increase is driven by regulation of phosphofructokinase (PFK), the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme: ATP and citrate (both more abundant when the Krebs cycle/ETC are active) are allosteric inhibitors of PFK, while AMP and ADP (more abundant when ATP production falls under anaerobic conditions) are allosteric activators. Anaerobically, falling ATP/citrate and rising AMP/ADP relieve PFK inhibition and activate it, ramping up glycolytic rate to compensate for the far lower ATP yield per glucose molecule.

rubric.minimum_fix: Alcoholic: pyruvate -> acetaldehyde + CO2 -> ethanol + NAD+. Lactic acid: pyruvate -> lactate + NAD+. Purpose of both: regenerate NAD+ to allow glycolysis to continue producing ATP without O2.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation pathways and explain the metabolic purpose they share.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Alcoholic fermentation (yeast): glucose -> 2 pyruvate -> 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO2 -> 2 ethanol + 2 NAD+; net C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + 2 ATP; CO2 is a byproduct. (ii) Lactic acid fermentation (exercising muscle): glucose -> 2 pyruvate -> 2 lactate + 2 NAD+; net C6H12O6 -> 2 C3H6O3 + 2 ATP; no CO2 produced; lactate can be exported to the liver (Cori cycle). Purpose shared by both pathways: regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue producing ATP anaerobically -- not to make lactate/ethanol as an end in itself. 1 pt for correct pathway/products for both types; 1 pt for correctly stating the shared metabolic purpose as NAD+ regeneration.

rubric.minimum_fix: Claim is incorrect. ATP is produced by glycolysis (substrate-level phosphorylation), NOT by fermentation reactions. Fermentation (pyruvate → lactate or ethanol) directly regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH — it produces no ATP itself. Fermentation enables glycolysis to continue by preventing NADH accumulation.
accepted_variants: fermentation does not produce ATP directly
enabling glycolysis not directly producing ATP
rubric.learner_facing_text: Evaluate the claim that fermentation directly produces ATP; clarify which step produces ATP.
rubric.evidence_requirements: The claim is INCORRECT as stated. ATP is produced by GLYCOLYSIS (substrate-level phosphorylation at phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps), NOT by the fermentation reactions themselves. The fermentation reactions (pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂, or pyruvate → lactate) produce NO ATP directly — they are redox reactions that recycle NAD⁺ by oxidizing NADH. The purpose of fermentation is to regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue to operate and produce ATP. Without NAD⁺ regeneration, the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis would halt (requires NAD⁺ as electron acceptor) → glycolysis stops → no more ATP from glycolysis. Distinction matters: the ATP comes from glycolysis; fermentation is a supporting reaction that enables glycolysis to keep running by preventing NADH accumulation. This is why some students confuse fermentation with energy production — it enables energy production (glycolysis) rather than performing it directly.

rubric.minimum_fix: (i) Aerobic CO₂: pyruvate oxidation + Krebs. Anaerobic CO₂: pyruvate decarboxylase only (alcoholic fermentation). (ii) Higher anaerobic CO₂: need 4× more glucose to generate ATP → more decarboxylation steps → more CO₂ per hour. (iii) Cyanide: ETC blocked → forced anaerobic → CO₂ increases to anaerobic levels.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain CO₂ under both conditions; explain higher anaerobic rate; predict cyanide effect.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) CO₂ sources: Aerobic — CO₂ released in pyruvate oxidation (1 CO₂ per pyruvate) and Krebs cycle (2 CO₂ per acetyl-CoA × 2 turns = 4 CO₂ total). Anaerobic — CO₂ released only in pyruvate → acetaldehyde step (1 CO₂ per pyruvate; 2 per glucose) by pyruvate decarboxylase. No CO₂ from lactic acid fermentation. Yeast do alcoholic fermentation, so CO₂ is produced anaerobically. (ii) Higher CO₂ anaerobically (8.5 vs. 3.0 mmol/hr/g): despite less ATP per glucose (2 vs. ~30), yeast must consume ~4× more glucose per hour to maintain adequate ATP production → more glucose molecules processed → more total fermentative CO₂ released per hour → higher CO₂ production rate. (iii) Cyanide (Complex IV inhibitor): blocks O₂ from being reduced → ETC halts → aerobic respiration stops → yeast switch to fermentation → CO₂ production would INCREASE toward anaerobic levels (Pasteur effect in reverse); the yeast, now functionally anaerobic, ferment glucose rapidly → high CO₂ output.

rubric.minimum_fix: Claim outdated: lactate does not cause muscle fatigue. Actual causes: H⁺ accumulation (from ATP hydrolysis, not from lactate) lowers pH → inhibits enzymes, reduces Ca²⁺ sensitivity; inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation impairs cross-bridge cycling; phosphocreatine depletion. Lactate itself may buffer acidosis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Evaluate "lactic acid burns muscle" claim; explain actual cause of muscle fatigue.
rubric.evidence_requirements: The claim is OUTDATED and largely incorrect. Current understanding: lactate (lactic acid) itself does not cause muscle fatigue or burning sensation. Lactate is a fuel that can be oxidized by heart and oxidative muscle fibers, and the Cori cycle converts lactate to glucose in the liver. Actual causes of muscle fatigue during intense exercise: (1) Inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation: Pi released from ATP hydrolysis accumulates in the muscle; Pi inhibits cross-bridge cycling (reduces force per cross-bridge) and may block calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum → reduced force production; (2) Acidosis: excess H⁺ (from ATP hydrolysis: ATP → ADP + Pi + H⁺) lowers intracellular pH → inhibits enzyme activity and reduces calcium sensitivity of troponin → reduced force. The burning sensation is from H⁺ (acid), not lactate per se. (3) Depletion of phosphocreatine and glycogen; (4) ADP accumulation. Lactate correlates with fatigue (produced alongside H⁺ under anaerobic conditions) but does not cause it. Some evidence suggests lactate may actually buffer acidosis by consuming H⁺ in the LDH reaction. 1 pt for correctly identifying the claim as outdated/incorrect; 1 pt for explaining actual fatigue mechanisms (H⁺, Pi accumulation).

question.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Compare alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation, and explain the metabolic purpose both pathways share.

Part B: A claim states that fermentation directly produces ATP from the reactions shown in the stimulus. Evaluate this claim: identify which step, if any, produces ATP directly, and clarify where most of a cell's ATP actually comes from when oxygen is available.

Part C: Using Table 1, explain the CO₂ production values under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, explain why the anaerobic rate is higher, and predict the CO₂ production rate for the aerobic + cyanide condition, given that cyanide blocks the electron transport chain.

Part D: A common claim is that lactic acid directly causes the burning sensation in fatigued muscles. Evaluate this claim and explain what most directly causes muscle fatigue during intense anaerobic exercise.
question.stimulus:
Table 1: CO₂ production by yeast
Condition                    | CO₂ production (mmol/hr/g)
Aerobic (glucose)            |        3.0
Anaerobic (glucose)          |        8.5
Aerobic (glucose + cyanide)  |        ?

Alcoholic fermentation reactions:
Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase)
2 Acetaldehyde + 2 NADH → 2 ethanol + 2 NAD⁺ (alcohol dehydrogenase)

Lactic acid fermentation:
Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 lactate (lactate dehydrogenase)
(No CO₂ produced in lactic acid fermentation)

existing_canonical_answer.canonical_answer_1:
(a) Alcoholic fermentation (yeast): Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation) and 2 NADH. Pyruvate decarboxylase removes a carboxyl group from each pyruvate, releasing CO2 and forming acetaldehyde. Alcohol dehydrogenase then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ in the process. Net reaction: glucose to 2 ethanol + 2 CO2. Lactic acid fermentation (exercising muscle): glycolysis proceeds identically (2 ATP, 2 NADH). Lactate dehydrogenase directly reduces pyruvate to lactate, oxidizing NADH to NAD+; no CO2 is released. In both pathways, the enzyme catalyzing the final, defining step is lactate dehydrogenase (muscle) or alcohol dehydrogenase (yeast), and the metabolic purpose in both cases is identical: regenerate NAD+ so that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in glycolysis can keep functioning, allowing glycolysis (the only ATP-producing step available without O2) to continue.

(b) The claim is false/misleading. The reduction of pyruvate/acetaldehyde to lactate/ethanol (the fermentation step itself) produces zero ATP — it is purely a redox (NADH to NAD+) reaction with no phosphorylation of ADP. The actual ATP-producing step is glycolysis, specifically the substrate-level phosphorylation reactions catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase, which occur before fermentation and do not themselves require O2 or fermentation. Fermentation's real function is to regenerate the NAD+ consumed by glycolysis, indirectly sustaining ATP production by keeping glycolysis running. The distinction matters because it correctly locates anaerobic ATP synthesis in glycolysis (substrate-level phosphorylation), not in the fermentation reaction, which is bioenergetically neutral for ATP.

(c)(i) Yeast produce CO2 aerobically via two decarboxylation-based processes: pyruvate oxidation (pyruvate to acetyl-CoA + CO2) and the Krebs cycle (isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase steps). Anaerobically, yeast produce CO2 via pyruvate decarboxylase in alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate to acetaldehyde + CO2).
(ii) The anaerobic CO2 rate is higher because anaerobic ATP yield per glucose (2 ATP via glycolysis) is far lower than the aerobic yield (~30 ATP), so to meet the same energy demand yeast must process glucose at a much higher rate anaerobically. Even though aerobic respiration releases more CO2 per glucose molecule (6 CO2 vs. 2 CO2 in fermentation), the much higher glucose flux anaerobically results in a higher overall CO2 production rate per unit time.
(iii) Cyanide blocks Complex IV, halting electron flow and stopping oxidative phosphorylation even in the presence of O2. Yeast would respond as if anaerobic: glycolytic flux would increase (loss of ATP/citrate-mediated PFK inhibition) and cells would shift to alcoholic fermentation to regenerate NAD+. CO2 production would initially drop (loss of the 6 CO2/glucose from pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle) but then rise again, approaching anaerobic-like rates, as fermentation-driven glycolytic flux increases and CO2 is produced via pyruvate decarboxylase.

(d) The coach's claim is not supported by current physiology. Lactate itself is not a metabolic "waste" that directly damages muscle; it can even be used as fuel by muscle and other tissues (e.g., the heart, liver via the Cori cycle). Lactate production and fatigue are correlated (both increase during intense anaerobic exercise) because they share the same underlying cause — high rates of anaerobic glycolysis — but lactate itself is not the causal agent of fatigue.

rubric.minimum_fix: Insulin binds receptor → RTK auto-phosphorylation → IRS-1 phosphorylated → PI3K activated → PIP2→PIP3 → Akt (PKB) activated → AS160 phosphorylated → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with plasma membrane → glucose uptake.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe insulin → RTK → IRS-1 → PI3K → Akt → GLUT4 pathway in sequence.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Correct pathway sequence: (1) Insulin binds to the extracellular α-subunit of the insulin receptor → conformational change. (2) β-subunit cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domains auto-phosphorylate each other (transautophosphorylation) → kinase becomes active. (3) Activated receptor phosphorylates IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) on multiple tyrosines. (4) Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits and activates PI3K (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase). (5) PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3 at inner leaflet of plasma membrane. (6) PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the membrane; PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. (7) Active Akt phosphorylates AS160 (a GTPase-activating protein for Rab GTPases) → inactivates AS160 → Rab GTPases remain GTP-bound → GLUT4-containing vesicles traffic to and fuse with plasma membrane → increased glucose uptake. 1 pt for RTK activation mechanism (auto-phosphorylation, IRS-1 phosphorylation); 1 pt for PI3K→PIP3→Akt→GLUT4 mechanism.

rubric.minimum_fix: RTK (insulin): intrinsic tyrosine kinase, PIP3/Akt amplification, effect = glucose uptake / glycogen synthesis. GPCR (epinephrine): 7-TM receptor, Gα → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA, effect = glycogenolysis / fight-or-flight response.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare RTK (insulin) and GPCR (epinephrine) pathways on receptor type, second messenger, and physiological effect.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Insulin receptor (RTK): (i) Transmembrane receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; single-pass (dimer) transmembrane; extracellular ligand-binding domain + intracellular kinase domain. (ii) Primary amplifier: PIP3 (membrane phospholipid second messenger) → activates Akt; no classical second messenger like cAMP; amplification through phosphorylation cascade. (iii) Physiological effect in liver: GLUT4 insertion → increased glucose uptake; glycogen synthase activated → glycogen synthesis; protein synthesis via mTOR. β-adrenergic receptor (GPCR): (i) 7-transmembrane receptor coupled to G-protein; no intrinsic catalytic activity; activates associated Gα protein. (ii) Primary second messenger: cAMP (produced by adenylyl cyclase activated by Gα-GTP) → activates PKA (protein kinase A) → phosphorylates multiple targets. (iii) Physiological effect in skeletal muscle: PKA activates phosphorylase kinase → activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) → glucose-1-phosphate → glycolysis → ATP for fight-or-flight. 1 pt per pathway with all 3 elements correct.

rubric.minimum_fix: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: hypoglycemia, excess glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis even without food. (2) Proliferation: mTOR and Akt constitutively active → cell growth, reduced apoptosis, tumor-like proliferation. (3) Gene expression: FOXO transcription factors constitutively inhibited → reduced gluconeogenesis genes, reduced apoptosis genes.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict three consequences of constitutively active insulin receptor.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: cells would constitutively import glucose (GLUT4 always at surface in insulin-sensitive cells) → increased glycolysis and glycogen synthesis → hypoglycemia (low blood glucose) as cells deplete blood glucose even in fasting state; excess acetyl-CoA → lipogenesis → excess fat storage. (2) Cell proliferation: Akt constitutively active → phosphorylates and inactivates GSK-3 → β-catenin accumulates → activates Wnt target genes promoting cell division; mTOR constitutively active → enhanced protein synthesis and cell growth; FOXO transcription factors constitutively inactivated → reduced expression of p27 (CDK inhibitor) and other cell cycle brakes → excessive cell proliferation → potential tumor formation. (3) Gene expression: constitutive Akt inactivates FOXO → reduced FOXO-dependent transcription (genes for gluconeogenesis, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis suppressed); mTOR promotes ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis genes; constitutive growth signals mimic oncogenic transformation. Award 1 pt per two well-explained consequences, max 2 pts.

rubric.minimum_fix: (i) HER2 overexpression: spontaneous dimerization → constitutive kinase activity → continuous RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling without growth factor. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: cannot hydrolyze GTP → always active → constitutive MAPK → proliferation. (iii) PTEN loss: cannot convert PIP3→PIP2 → PIP3 accumulates → Akt always active → mTOR → proliferation (lost tumor suppressor).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how HER2 overexpression, Ras-GTP lock, and PTEN loss each contribute to cancer.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) HER2 overexpression: HER2 (ErbB2) is an RTK that forms dimers with other EGF family receptors; overexpression increases probability of spontaneous dimerization and auto-phosphorylation even without growth factor binding → constitutive downstream signaling (Ras→MAPK, PI3K→Akt) → constant proliferation signal. Also, more receptors means stronger amplified response to any ligand. Targeted by trastuzumab (Herceptin) antibody therapy. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: Ras is a small GTPase; normally GTP-Ras is active and stimulates proliferation (through MAPK cascade); Ras-GAP proteins hydrolyze GTP → GDP to inactivate Ras. A mutation preventing GTP hydrolysis (e.g., G12V mutation in KRAS) locks Ras in the active GTP-bound state → constitutive MAPK activation → continuous proliferation signal regardless of whether growth factor receptor is active. ~30% of human cancers have Ras mutations. (iii) PTEN loss: PTEN is a phosphatase that converts PIP3 back to PIP2 (antagonizes PI3K). Loss-of-function mutation → PIP3 accumulates constitutively → Akt constitutively active → mTOR always on → cell growth, survival, proliferation unchecked → tumor suppressor function lost (PTEN is a tumor suppressor). 1 pt per any two mechanisms with correct molecular detail.

question.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the information provided, describe the mechanism by which insulin binding triggers GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane. Trace the signaling pathway from insulin binding at the receptor through to glucose uptake.

Part B: Compare the insulin/receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathway to the epinephrine/G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) pathway described. For each pathway, identify: the receptor type and location, the primary second messenger or amplification step, and one physiological effect.

Part C: Suppose a mutation causes the insulin receptor to be constitutively (continuously) active, even in the absence of insulin. Predict THREE consequences of this mutation for the cell, addressing metabolic effects, cell proliferation, and gene expression.

Part D: Several distinct mutations can produce excessive, insulin-independent growth signaling in cancer cells. For EACH of the following, explain how the described change leads to chronic activation of a growth-signaling pathway:
(i) Overexpression of the HER2 receptor
(ii) A Ras protein locked in its GTP-bound form
(iii) Loss-of-function mutation in the PTEN gene
question.stimulus:
Insulin signaling pathway:
• Insulin binds → receptor α-subunits change conformation
• β-subunit cytoplasmic tails auto-phosphorylate tyrosines (kinase activation)
• IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) binds and is phosphorylated by receptor
• PI3K recruited → phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3
• PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt → PDK1 phosphorylates/activates Akt
• Active Akt phosphorylates downstream targets:
  – Phosphorylates AS160 → GLUT4 vesicle fusion with plasma membrane
  – Phosphorylates and inhibits GSK-3 → activates glycogen synthase
  – Activates mTOR → promotes protein synthesis
  – Phosphorylates and inactivates FOXO transcription factors

GPCR comparison:
• β-adrenergic receptor + epinephrine → Gα-GTP → adenylyl cyclase activated
• cAMP produced → PKA activated → multiple downstream phosphorylations

existing_canonical_answer.canonical_answer_1:
(a) Insulin binds the alpha-subunits of the insulin receptor, causing a conformational change that activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the beta-subunits; the beta-subunits trans-autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. These phosphotyrosines serve as docking sites that recruit and phosphorylate IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1). Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits PI3K via SH2 domains; PI3K phosphorylates membrane PIP2 to PIP3. PIP3 recruits both PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the plasma membrane, where PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. Active Akt phosphorylates AS160, inhibiting its normal suppression of Rab GTPases; this permits GLUT4-containing vesicles to translocate to and fuse with the plasma membrane, inserting GLUT4 glucose transporters and enabling glucose uptake.

(b) Insulin/RTK pathway: receptor type is a single-pass transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase located on the cell surface; the primary second messenger/amplifier is the PI3K to PIP3 to Akt phosphorylation cascade; physiological effect includes GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake (also glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis via mTOR). Epinephrine/GPCR (beta-adrenergic) pathway: receptor type is a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface, coupled to a Gs protein; the second messenger is cyclic AMP (cAMP), produced by adenylyl cyclase and activating protein kinase A (PKA); physiological effect includes glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) in liver/muscle via PKA-mediated activation of glycogen phosphorylase kinase, raising blood glucose as part of the fight-or-flight response.

(c) Three consequences of a constitutively active insulin receptor: (1) Metabolic effects — continuous Akt activation drives ongoing GLUT4 translocation and glycogen synthase activation (via GSK-3 inhibition), causing excessive, insulin-independent glucose uptake and storage, risking hypoglycemia and disrupted glucose homeostasis. (2) Cell proliferation — sustained activation of Akt/mTOR (and likely the parallel Ras/MAPK branch downstream of the RTK) promotes continuous protein synthesis and cell growth signals, potentially driving uncontrolled proliferation. (3) Gene expression effects — continuous phosphorylation and inactivation of FOXO transcription factors (which normally activate genes for gluconeogenesis and stress response/apoptosis when unphosphorylated) suppresses these FOXO target genes, altering glucose production pathways and reducing normal apoptotic/stress responses, which could favor unchecked cell survival.

(d)(i) HER2 overexpression: more receptor molecules on the cell surface increases the likelihood of ligand-independent receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, chronically activating downstream growth pathways (Ras/MAPK, PI3K/Akt) even without normal levels of growth factor, driving continuous proliferation signaling.
(ii) Ras locked in GTP-bound form: Ras normally functions as a molecular switch, active when GTP-bound and inactivated when it hydrolyzes GTP to GDP (assisted by GAPs); a mutation that prevents GTP hydrolysis leaves Ras permanently active, continuously stimulating the MAPK/ERK cascade and driving persistent proliferation signals to the nucleus regardless of upstream receptor activation.
(iii) PTEN loss-of-function: PTEN normally converts PIP3 back to PIP2, acting as a brake on the PI3K/Akt pathway; without functional PTEN, PIP3 accumulates unchecked, causing constitutive Akt activation and continuous pro-growth, pro-survival, anti-apoptotic signaling that drives uncontrolled proliferation and resistance to programmed cell death.

rubric.minimum_fix: X-linked recessive. Evidence: only males affected; skip-generation transmission; unaffected parents have affected sons. Genotypes: I-1 = X^A Y; I-2 = X^A X^a; II-3 = X^a Y; II-4 = X^A X^a. Probability affected female = 1/4 (25%).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Determine mode of inheritance; assign genotypes; calculate probability of affected female offspring.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) X-linked recessive. Evidence: (1) Only males are affected (II-3, III-1) — X-linked recessive affects males more frequently than females because males are hemizygous; (2) Affected son III-1 was born to two unaffected parents (II-4 and II-5) → trait skipped a generation → characteristic of recessive; (3) Affected II-3 had an unaffected father (I-1) — this rules out Y-linked (which would affect all sons of affected fathers); (4) I-2 must be a carrier (unaffected female with affected son II-3). Also rules out autosomal: autosomal recessive would give equal sex ratios; autosomal dominant would show affected in every generation if parents are affected. (ii) Genotypes: I-1: X^A Y (unaffected male, no allele to give son affected); I-2: X^A X^a (carrier female — must carry X^a to pass to affected son II-3); II-3: X^a Y (affected male); II-4: X^A X^a (carrier — must carry X^a to have affected son III-1, and her husband II-5 is X^A Y unaffected so son must have gotten X^a from her). (iii) Cross II-4 (X^A X^a) × II-3 (X^a Y): Possible offspring: X^A X^a (carrier female), X^a X^a (affected female), X^A Y (normal male), X^a Y (affected male). Probability affected female = X^a X^a = 1/4 = 25%.

rubric.minimum_fix: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes (only one X, no second allele on Y). A single recessive allele causes expression in males. Females (XX) need two copies of the recessive allele (homozygous) to be affected. Single-carrier females are unaffected. Therefore males affected much more frequently.
accepted_variants: Y does not carry X-linked alleles
single recessive allele expresses in males
dominant allele masks recessive in heterozygous female
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain molecular basis of higher male frequency for X-linked recessive traits using hemizygosity.
rubric.evidence_requirements: Hemizygosity: males have only one X chromosome and one Y chromosome (XY). The Y chromosome does not carry most genes present on the X chromosome (the non-pseudoautosomal region of Y is distinct). Therefore, for X-linked genes, males have only ONE copy of the allele (hemizygous) — there is no second allele on a homolog to mask the recessive allele's phenotypic effect. For X-linked recessive conditions: a male who inherits even one copy of the recessive allele (X^a Y) will be affected, because there is no corresponding dominant allele on the Y to compensate. For females: they have two X chromosomes (XX), so a female with one recessive allele (X^A X^a) is a heterozygous CARRIER — the dominant X^A allele produces sufficient functional protein to mask the recessive phenotype. A female must be homozygous recessive (X^a X^a) to be affected, requiring inheritance of the recessive allele from BOTH parents. This is much less probable than a male inheriting a single recessive allele. Example: red-green color blindness affects ~8% of males but only ~0.5% of females because female frequency ≈ (male frequency)² (Hardy-Weinberg).

rubric.minimum_fix: Timing: early embryo (~day 12-16), random choice in each cell (maternal or paternal X). Mechanism: XIST gene transcribes lncRNA that coats inactive X → recruits Polycomb proteins → histone methylation → DNA methylation → Barr body. Clonal: epigenetic marks copied at each cell division → all daughter cells have same inactive X.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain X-inactivation: timing, choice, molecular mechanism, and clonal inheritance.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Timing and choice: X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development — in placental mammals, around days 12-16 in humans (at the blastocyst → post-implantation stage, around the time of gastrulation; some texts say 100-cell stage). In each somatic cell of the early embryo, ONE X chromosome is randomly inactivated — either the maternal X or the paternal X is chosen with equal probability. (Note: in extra-embryonic cells like trophoblast, the paternal X is preferentially inactivated — imprinted X-inactivation.) After the initial choice is made independently in each cell, it is maintained in all descendants. (ii) Molecular mechanism: the XIST gene (X-Inactive Specific Transcript) on the X chromosome to be inactivated is transcribed and produces a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) called XIST (or Xist in mice). XIST RNA coats the inactive X chromosome in cis (spreads along the chromosome it is transcribed from). XIST RNA recruits chromatin-remodeling proteins (Polycomb group proteins) → histone modifications (H3K27 methylation, H3K9 methylation, loss of H3 acetylation) → heterochromatin formation → DNA methylation of CpG islands at gene promoters → gene silencing. The inactive X condenses into a dense structure called the Barr body (sex chromatin). (iii) Permanence and clonal inheritance: once X is inactivated, epigenetic marks (DNA methylation and histone modifications) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and cell division → every daughter cell inherits the same inactive X → the inactivation pattern is clonally inherited for the lifetime of the organism. The XIST RNA continues to be expressed from the inactive X to maintain silencing. This is why X-inactivation is an irreversible epigenetic modification in somatic cells. 1 pt per two sub-parts correctly addressed.

question.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The pedigree in Figure 1 shows the inheritance of a trait across three generations. Affected individuals are shaded. Determine the most likely mode of inheritance and justify your answer by identifying at least TWO pedigree observations that support your conclusion. Assign genotypes to individuals I-1, I-2, II-3 (an affected male), and II-4 (an unaffected female who has an affected son). Calculate the probability that a child of II-4 and II-3 will be an affected female.

Part B: Males with X-linked recessive conditions are affected at a much higher frequency than females. Explain the molecular and genetic basis for this sex difference, using hemizygosity in your explanation.

Part C: Explain X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis) in female mammals. Describe when X-inactivation occurs in development and how the choice of which X is inactivated is made. Describe the molecular mechanism of X-inactivation, naming the gene responsible and the RNA molecule involved. Explain why X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited.

Part D: A tortoiseshell cat has patches of orange and black fur. The gene for orange/black fur color is X-linked. Explain why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female. Explain why the patches of orange and black fur are large rather than a uniform blended color. Predict the coat color pattern of a female cat that is homozygous for the orange allele.
question.stimulus:
Pedigree — Figure 1 (described):
Generation I:   I-1 (unaffected male) × I-2 (unaffected female)
Generation II:  II-1 (unaffected female), II-2 (unaffected male),
                II-3 (AFFECTED male), II-4 (unaffected female),
                II-5 (unaffected male)
Generation III: III-1 (AFFECTED male, son of II-4 and II-5)
                III-2 (unaffected female, daughter of II-4 and II-5)

Note: No affected females in pedigree.
Affected: II-3 (male), III-1 (male, son of II-4 and unaffected II-5)

X-linked gene notation:
• X^A = dominant / unaffected allele
• X^a = recessive / affected allele
• Females: X^A X^A (normal), X^A X^a (carrier), X^a X^a (affected)
• Males: X^A Y (normal), X^a Y (affected)

existing_canonical_answer.canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Most likely mode of inheritance: X-linked recessive. Two supporting pedigree observations: (1) only males are affected (no affected females appear anywhere in the pedigree), consistent with a recessive allele on the X chromosome where males need only one copy (hemizygous) to be affected while females need two copies; (2) the trait appears to skip a generation through an unaffected carrier female (II-4, unaffected, yet has an affected son III-1), which is the classic X-linked recessive pattern of transmission through unaffected carrier mothers rather than direct parent-to-offspring transmission in every generation.
(ii) Genotypes: I-1 = X^A Y (unaffected male); I-2 = X^A X^a (obligate carrier, since she must have transmitted the recessive allele that appears in affected descendants); II-3 = X^a Y (affected male); II-4 = X^A X^a (unaffected carrier female, confirmed by having an affected son).
(iii) Cross II-4 (X^A X^a, carrier female) x II-3 (X^a Y, affected male) gives offspring: 1/4 X^A X^a (carrier female), 1/4 X^a X^a (affected female), 1/4 X^A Y (unaffected male), 1/4 X^a Y (affected male). The probability of an affected female (X^a X^a) is 1/4 (25%): the affected father II-3 always contributes X^a to every daughter, and the carrier mother II-4 contributes X^a to half of her offspring, so a daughter is affected only if she also receives X^a from her mother -- 1/2 (mother's X^a) x 1 (father's obligate X^a) = 1/4.

(b) Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes -- they have only a single X chromosome (paired with a Y chromosome that lacks a homologous allele for most X-linked genes), so a single copy of a recessive allele is sufficient to produce the affected phenotype in males, with no second allele to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes, so a single recessive allele is typically masked by a normal dominant allele on the other X chromosome (heterozygous carrier females are unaffected); females must inherit the recessive allele from both parents to be affected, which is much less likely, especially for rare alleles, explaining the much higher frequency of affected males.

(c)(i) X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development, around the blastocyst stage (approximately day 5-6 in humans), independently in each cell of the female embryo. The choice of which X chromosome (maternal or paternal) is inactivated in each cell is random.
(ii) The Xist gene, located on the X chromosome destined to be inactivated, is upregulated and transcribes a long non-coding RNA (Xist RNA) that coats that X chromosome in cis; this recruits chromatin-modifying complexes that establish heterochromatin (histone deacetylation and methylation, DNA methylation), condensing that chromosome into a transcriptionally silent Barr body.
(iii) X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited because once a given cell inactivates a specific X chromosome, the epigenetic marks (including DNA methylation patterns) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and passed on to all of that cell's mitotic descendants, so each clonal lineage of cells maintains the same inactivated X, producing stable patches of tissue expressing only one parental X allele.

(d)(i) Tortoiseshell cats are almost always female because the orange/black coat color gene is X-linked; a heterozygous female undergoes random X-inactivation, creating two populations of cells -- some expressing the orange allele, others the black allele -- producing a patched, two-color coat. Males are hemizygous (XY) and carry only one allele, so they are uniformly either orange or black (except in rare XXY males).
(ii) The patches are large rather than finely blended because X-inactivation happens early in development when the embryo consists of relatively few cells; each of those early cells' clonal descendants (forming a large contiguous patch of tissue) all inherit the same inactivated X, so entire regions of skin trace back to a single early progenitor with one particular X active, producing large, blocky patches rather than a fine intermixed pattern.
(iii) A female homozygous for the orange allele would be entirely orange, with no black patches, because every cell expresses the orange allele regardless of which X chromosome is inactivated.

rubric.minimum_fix: TFIID (TBP binds TATA box) and TFIIH (helicase opens DNA, CTD kinase activates RNA pol II) assemble PIC. Enhancer: activators bind → DNA loops (cohesin/CTCF) → enhancer contacts promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → increased transcription.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe PIC assembly at eukaryotic promoter naming two GTFs; explain enhancer-Mediator mechanism.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) PIC assembly: (1) A pioneer transcription factor or general factor recognizes the TATA box (core promoter element ~25 bp upstream of TSS) → TFIID (containing TBP, TATA-Binding Protein) binds the TATA box; TBP bends DNA. (2) TFIIA and TFIIB are recruited → TFIIB positions RNA pol II. (3) TFIIF enters with RNA pol II → stabilizes RNA pol II at promoter. (4) TFIIE and TFIIH join → TFIIH has helicase activity to unwind DNA at TSS (open complex formation) and kinase activity to phosphorylate the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA pol II → triggers elongation. Two GTFs to name: TFIID (TBP subunit recognizes TATA box), TFIIH (helicase opens DNA and CTD kinase activates polymerase). (ii) Enhancer mechanism: activator proteins bind the enhancer element via their DNA-binding domains. The activation domains of activators recruit coactivators and Mediator complex. The chromatin between enhancer and promoter loops around (enhancer-promoter looping, mediated by cohesin and CTCF proteins) → brings the activator-Mediator complex into contact with the PIC at the promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → stimulates transcription initiation rate. This looping explains action at a distance (10 kb away). 1 pt for PIC assembly with two GTFs and roles; 1 pt for enhancer-looping-Mediator mechanism.

rubric.minimum_fix: Euchromatin: hyperacetylated histones (H3K4me3), loose chromatin. Heterochromatin: deacetylated histones (H3K9me3, H3K27me3), compact. HATs acetylate lysines → neutralize charge → looser chromatin → more transcription. HDACs remove acetyl → compact. HDAC inhibitor → all histones remain acetylated → global gene upregulation → silenced genes de-repressed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe euchromatin/heterochromatin histone modifications; HAT/HDAC mechanisms; predict HDAC inhibitor effect.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Euchromatin vs. heterochromatin at histone level: Euchromatin — histones are hyperacetylated (acetyl groups on lysine residues of H3 and H4 N-terminal tails) and have active histone methylation marks (H3K4me3 at promoters); chromatin is loose and accessible. Heterochromatin — histones are hypoacetylated (deacetylated), have repressive methylation marks (H3K9me3, H3K27me3); histone H1 (linker histone) compacts chromatin further; chromatin is condensed, DNA inaccessible. (ii) HAT/HDAC mechanism: HATs (histone acetyltransferases) add acetyl groups to histone lysine residues → neutralizes positive charge of lysine → reduces attraction between histones and negatively charged DNA → chromatin loosens (nucleosome-DNA interaction weakened) → DNA more accessible to transcription machinery → transcription increases. HDACs (histone deacetylases) remove acetyl groups → lysines revert to positive charge → stronger histone-DNA interactions → chromatin compacts → transcription decreases. (iii) Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor) effect: HDACs cannot remove acetyl groups → histones remain hyperacetylated → chromatin stays loose/open → global increase in transcription of many genes, including genes normally kept silenced. Genes under active repression via deacetylation would be de-repressed. Effect: widespread upregulation of gene expression; some previously silenced genes (tumor suppressors, differentiation genes) may be reactivated. This is why HDAC inhibitors are investigated as cancer therapies. 1 pt for euchromatin/heterochromatin marks with mechanism; 1 pt for correct HDAC inhibitor prediction with reasoning.

rubric.minimum_fix: DBD alone: binding DNA insufficient for activation. ADs differ in strength; AD3 > AD1 > AD2. AD1+AD3 synergistic (203 > 132) = combinatorial activation. AD3-Mediator interaction: recruits Mediator to promoter → bridges activator to RNA pol II → stimulates PIC assembly or CTD phosphorylation → increased transcription.
accepted_variants: Mediator bridges activator to RNA pol II
rubric.learner_facing_text: Interpret domain fusion experiment data; explain Mediator interaction mechanism.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) DBD alone (expression = 1, baseline): the DNA-binding domain alone can bind the promoter but does NOT activate transcription — it shows that DNA binding is necessary but not sufficient for transcription activation. Simply recruiting a protein to the DNA does not stimulate RNA pol II. Transcriptional activation requires a separate activation domain. (ii) Activation domain results: activation domains differ in strength (AD3 > AD1 > AD2); the activation domain is the functional module responsible for stimulating transcription, independent of what DNA it is bound to (domain swap experiment works). Combining AD1 + AD3 gives superadditive (synergistic) activation (203 > 45+87 = 132) — demonstrates that multiple activation domains can work cooperatively (combinatorial activation), perhaps by recruiting different coactivators simultaneously. (iii) Mediator interaction of AD3: if AD3 physically contacts the Mediator complex, AD3 recruits Mediator to the promoter → Mediator acts as a bridge between activators and the general transcription machinery → Mediator interacts with RNA pol II CTD → stimulates assembly of the PIC or transition from initiation to productive elongation (CTD phosphorylation) → increased transcription. AD3's stronger activation could be because it makes particularly favorable contacts with Mediator subunits. 1 pt for correct interpretations of DBD alone + AD results; 1 pt for Mediator mechanism.

rubric.minimum_fix: Combinatorial TF control: different cell types have different TF combinations; each gene requires a specific TF combination; same genome interpreted differently per cell type. Epigenetic inheritance: chromatin marks (DNA methylation, H3K27me3) copied at each division; liver cell daughters remain liver cells; self-perpetuating chromatin states stabilize cell identity.
accepted_variants: different TF combinations per cell type
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain cell-type-specific expression via combinatorial TF control and epigenetic inheritance.
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Combinatorial control by transcription factors: different cell types express different subsets of transcription factors; the combination of TFs present in a cell determines which genes are active. Gene A may require TF1 + TF2 + TF3 to be activated; Gene B requires TF1 + TF4. A neuron expresses TF1+TF2+TF3 (→ Gene A on, Gene B off); a muscle cell expresses TF1+TF4 (→ Gene A off, Gene B on). With as few as 10 different TFs, the combinatorial possibilities (2^10 = 1024 combinations) can specify hundreds of distinct cell identities. The same promoter is interpreted differently depending on which TFs are present → same genome, different expression profiles. (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states: once a cell commits to a lineage, its chromatin state (which regions are euchromatic vs. heterochromatic, DNA methylation at CpG islands, Polycomb/Trithorax marks on histones) is faithfully copied at each cell division. Maintenance methyltransferases (DNMT1) re-methylate hemimethylated DNA after replication. Histone modifications are self-perpetuating (Polycomb group proteins recognize their own mark → spread to newly deposited histones). This ensures that a liver cell's daughter cells remain liver cells and do not become neurons — the gene expression program is inherited epigenetically without changes in DNA sequence. 1 pt per mechanism correctly explained with cellular specificity logic.

question.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Eukaryotic gene expression requires the coordinated action of transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, and chromatin remodeling. Describe the sequence of events that leads to the assembly of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) at a eukaryotic promoter and name TWO general transcription factors and their roles. Explain how an enhancer element located 10,000 base pairs upstream of a gene can stimulate transcription at the gene's promoter, including the role of activator proteins and Mediator.

Part B: Chromatin structure regulates access to DNA. Using Figure 1 (which shows the same gene in euchromatin vs. heterochromatin states): Describe the structural difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin at the level of histone modification. Explain how histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs) have opposite effects on transcription, including the mechanism by which acetylation opens chromatin. A researcher adds trichostatin A (an HDAC inhibitor) to cells. Predict and explain the effect on global gene expression.

Part C: Experiment: The researcher fuses the DNA-binding domain of a transcription factor to different activation domains and measures target gene expression. Results are shown in Table 1. What does the DNA-binding domain alone demonstrate about gene activation? What do the activation domain results reveal about how transcription is activated? The researcher finds that activation domain 3 interacts physically with the Mediator complex. Explain how this interaction could lead to increased transcription.

Part D: Explain how the following two mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific gene expression in a multicellular organism that has one genome but hundreds of distinct cell types: Combinatorial control by transcription factors and epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states.
question.stimulus:
Figure 1 (described):
• Euchromatin: beads-on-a-string appearance; histones visible as individual nucleosomes; 30nm fiber partially unfolded; gene accessible to RNA polymerase → gene ON
• Heterochromatin: highly compact; 300nm fiber; DNA wound tightly; gene inaccessible → gene OFF

Table 1: Transcription factor domain fusion experiment
Construct                    | Target gene expression (relative units)
DBD alone                    |         1 (baseline)
DBD + Activation Domain 1    |        45
DBD + Activation Domain 2    |        12
DBD + Activation Domain 3    |        87
DBD + AD1 + AD3              |       203

Note: DBD = DNA-binding domain; all constructs bind the same promoter sequence.

existing_canonical_answer.canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Pre-initiation complex (PIC) assembly: TFIID (via its TBP subunit) binds the TATA box in the promoter and bends the DNA, nucleating assembly of the complex; this recruits TFIIA and TFIIB, which stabilize TFIID binding and help correctly position RNA Polymerase II at the transcription start site. RNA Pol II is recruited together with TFIIF; TFIIE and TFIIH then join the complex. TFIIH has both helicase activity (unwinds the DNA at the start site, forming the transcription bubble) and kinase activity (phosphorylates the C-terminal domain, CTD, of RNA Pol II), which triggers promoter escape and the start of transcription. Two general transcription factors and their roles: TFIID (binds the TATA box via TBP, nucleates PIC assembly) and TFIIH (unwinds promoter DNA and phosphorylates the Pol II CTD to initiate transcription).
(ii) Enhancers act at a distance through DNA looping: activator proteins bind the enhancer sequence; the Mediator complex physically bridges these DNA-bound activators with the general transcription machinery (including RNA Pol II and the general transcription factors) assembled at the promoter, causing the intervening DNA to loop out so the enhancer and promoter come into close physical proximity despite being far apart in linear sequence. This interaction stabilizes PIC assembly at the promoter and increases the rate of transcription initiation.

(b)(i) Euchromatin has hyperacetylated histones, is loosely packed in a "beads-on-a-string" (10 nm fiber) conformation with accessible DNA. Heterochromatin has hypoacetylated (deacetylated) and often methylated histones (for example, H3K9 trimethylation), and is tightly compacted (30 nm+ fiber), rendering the DNA inaccessible.
(ii) Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) add acetyl groups to lysine residues on histone tails, neutralizing their positive charge; this weakens the electrostatic attraction between the histones and the negatively charged DNA backbone, loosening chromatin structure and increasing accessibility for transcription factors and RNA polymerase, thereby activating transcription. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove these acetyl groups, restoring the positive charge on histones, tightening histone-DNA interactions, condensing chromatin, and repressing transcription.
(iii) Trichostatin A inhibits HDACs, causing acetyl groups to accumulate on histones (global hyperacetylation). Chromatin becomes more open and accessible throughout the genome, which generally increases global gene expression, since more promoters and regulatory regions become accessible to transcription factors and RNA polymerase.

(c)(i) The DNA-binding domain alone produces only baseline expression (about 1), demonstrating that binding to the promoter DNA is necessary but not sufficient to activate transcription — the DBD can locate and occupy the target sequence but cannot itself recruit the machinery needed to activate transcription without an activation domain.
(ii) The different activation domains produce very different levels of activation (45, 12, 87), showing that activation is modular and that activation domains vary substantially in their ability to recruit and stimulate the transcriptional machinery, likely reflecting differences in the specific protein-protein interactions each domain can make with coactivators, chromatin remodelers, or Mediator. The combined AD1 + AD3 result (203) exceeding either domain alone demonstrates a synergistic (more than additive) effect when multiple activation domains act together.
(iii) Because Activation Domain 3 physically interacts with the Mediator complex, it can directly recruit Mediator to the promoter region; Mediator in turn helps recruit and stabilize RNA Polymerase II and the general transcription factors at the promoter, increasing the efficiency of PIC assembly and the rate of transcription initiation, explaining AD3's strong activation of gene expression (87 relative units).

(d)(i) Combinatorial control: different cell types express different combinations of transcription factors. A given gene's regulatory elements often require a specific combination of multiple transcription factors bound simultaneously to be activated, so the gene is only expressed in cell types that happen to express that particular combination of factors; this allows a relatively limited number of transcription factors to generate many distinct, cell-type-specific gene expression patterns combinatorially.
(ii) Epigenetic inheritance: the chromatin state (DNA methylation patterns and histone modifications) established at specific genes during differentiation is stably maintained and copied through successive rounds of DNA replication and mitosis, so a differentiated cell's daughter cells retain the same pattern of active and silenced genes as the parent cell — this preserves cell-type identity across many cell divisions without requiring the pattern of gene expression to be re-established from scratch in every generation of cells.
